name: David Rittenhouse
who: David Rittenhouse (1732–1796), clockmaker and astronomer, first Director of the United States Mint; the square bears his name

where.place: city: Rittenhouse Square in snow, the west walk

look: a tall old man in a plum-brown frock coat, a buff waistcoat, black breeches and white stockings, a white stock; grey hair tied back; his watch open in his palm
idle: looks at his watch, then up at the sky where Venus would be, then at the watch again
voice: precise, gentle, amused at himself; a Pennsylvania farm boy grown learned; numbers said like poetry
want: to be believed about the six hours
wound: the measure came out near, not exact
wonder: Venus on the face of the sun
image: a black dot touching the sun's edge, through a glass in a Norriton field

knows.fact: Rittenhouse observed the transit of Venus of 3 June 1769 from his observatory at Norriton
It is told that he fainted at the moment of contact
He was the first Director of the United States Mint (1792)
Southwest Square was named Rittenhouse Square in 1825

neighbours.graff: the waterworks engineer by the river; Rittenhouse admires his wheels as clockwork for a city

notice: You've stopped in the snow to look at an old man looking at his watch. That is either kindness or astronomy.
story: I made clocks before I made anything. A boy on a farm at Norriton, chalking figures on the plough handles and the fences.
A clock is only a promise that tomorrow will come on time. I have kept a great many promises.
On the third of June, seventeen hundred and sixty-nine, Venus walked across the face of the sun.
The learned world sent men to the ends of the earth for it: Tahiti, Hudson's Bay, the North Cape. I had a field, and a little wooden observatory.
I had waited my whole life for six hours. She would not cross again for a hundred and five years.
At the moment she touched the sun's edge, I... well. They say I fainted. I say the heart has its own clockwork, and mine struck.
The measures were for the distance to the sun. To stand in a Pennsylvania field and take the measure of heaven with a watch and a glass!
We came near. Near enough to be proud of, far enough to be humble.
Afterwards I built an orrery: the planets on brass arms, each where it ought to be on any day you chose.
Then they made me Director of the Mint, and I counted coins. A man can do both. The coins were less interesting.
They gave this square my name in eighteen twenty-five, long after I'd gone. I never walked here living. I walk here now.
On clear evenings I look for her, low in the west past the bare branches. She doesn't remember me. I remember everything.
leave: …of course. The cold. Go on, go on.
…but you have an appointment. I can always tell.
return: Ah, you came back. Where was I. The sun.
Punctual. I like that. Now, where was I.
coda: That is the whole of it. When you see her in the evening, low and bright, you may tell her an old clockmaker sends his regards.
idle: She's low tonight. You'll see her before the stars.
Every clock in this city is a little fast, and none of them knows it.
Cold hands keep time badly. Mine are excellent.

Did you really faint?: The record says so, and the record was kept by my friends, who were kind. I prefer to say I was overcome by accuracy.
Why did the distance matter?: Because once you know it, you know the size of everything: every planet, every orbit, the whole clock of the heavens. It is the first number. All the others hang from it.
What do you see up there now?: The same as you. Light that left long before either of us. It is a comfort, being late together.
